lessons.title: Wishes need subjunctive (quiero que…)
lessons.learn: After wishes and wants, Spanish switches mood: QUIERO QUE HABLES (I want you to speak). HABLES is SUBJUNCTIVE — for wishes, not facts. Pattern: QUIERO QUE + …ES.

grammar.title: Subjunctive after QUIERO QUE: hables
grammar.explain: QUIERO QUE + subjunctive: HABLAS (you speak, fact) → HABLES (wish). For -AR verbs: swap A→E: habla→hable, hablas→hables. Wishes live in the E-world!
mistakes: Saying QUIERO QUE HABLAS — wishes need HABLES (E, not A).
Using subjunctive for facts: VEO que hablas (fact, no switch).

dialogue.t: Quiero que hables con el jefe.
dialogue.r: KYEH-roh keh AH-blehs kohn ehl HEH-feh.
dialogue.en: I want you to talk to the boss.
Agreed.

lessons.title: News and reported speech
lessons.learn: Report what others say: DICE QUE VIENE (he says he is coming). DICE QUE + normal sentence. For past reports: DIJO QUE VINO (he said he came). News verbs: INFORMAR, ANUNCIAR, CONFIRMAR.

grammar.title: Reported speech: dice/dijo que…
grammar.explain: DICE QUE + sentence (he says that…). Past: DIJO QUE + past (he said that…). The rest of the sentence stays normal — only the intro verb moves in time.
grammar.pattern: dice que + present · dijo que + past

examples.en: The paper says it is raining.

mistakes: Moving the whole sentence to past: DIJO QUE VINO (only dijo moves back).
Forgetting QUE: DICE QUE viene, with QUE!

lessons.title: Conceder y rebatir: es cierto que…, aunque, sin embargo
lessons.learn: The Spanish rebuttal concedes first: ES CIERTO QUE … PERO … · AUNQUE …, SIN EMBARGO … The concession is a grammatical slot, not a decoration — and it decides the mood of the clause that follows.

grammar.title: Concession
grammar.pattern: es cierto que + indicative · aunque + indicative (fact) / subjunctive (hypothesis)
grammar.explain: Es cierto que la medida es popular, pero nadie ha medido su coste. Aunque llueva, saldremos (hypothesis → subjunctive). The mood of aunque is the argument: fact or supposition.

examples.t: Es cierto que es popular, pero tiene un coste.
examples.r: es SYEHR-toh keh es poh-poo-LAR, PEH-roh TYEH-neh oon KOS-teh.
examples.en: It is true that it is popular, but it has a cost.
Even if it rains, we will go.
However, one piece of data is missing.

mistakes.wrong: Es cierto que, pero sin embargo…
mistakes.why: One concessive per sentence; stacking cancels it.

dialogue.en: What do you think of the proposal?

dialogue.t: Es cierto que ahorra tiempo, pero el coste es alto.
dialogue.r: es SYEHR-toh keh ah-OH-rrah TYEHM-poh, PEH-roh el KOS-teh es AL-toh.
dialogue.en: It is true that it saves time, but the cost is high.
And your proposal?

dialogue.t: Sin embargo, creo que podemos probarlo un mes.
dialogue.r: seen em-BAR-goh, KREH-oh keh poh-DEH-mohs proh-BAR-loh oon mes.
dialogue.en: However, I think we can test it for a month.

lessons.title: Polite requests (conditional)
lessons.learn: Sound professional: ME GUSTARÍA (I would like), PODRÍA (could you…?). Conditional adds -ÍA to the whole verb: HABLARÍA, COMERÍA. ¿PODRÍA AYUDARME? = Could you help me?

grammar.title: Conditional: whole verb + ía
grammar.explain: HABLARÍA (I would speak), PODRÍA (I/he could), GUSTARÍA (would like). Same for all verbs — add -ÍA/-ÍAS/-ÍA to the infinitive. ME GUSTARÍA + verb = I would like to…
mistakes: Cutting the verb: HABLARÍA keeps -AR + ÍA.
Using QUIERO with strangers — GUSTARÍA is softer.

lessons.title: POR vs PARA (for)
lessons.learn: Two FORS! PARA = purpose/destination (PARA TI = for you, PARA MADRID = to Madrid). POR = cause/price/exchange (POR LA LLUVIA = because of rain, POR 10 EUROS = for 10 euros).

grammar.title: PARA = purpose · POR = cause
grammar.explain: PARA answers WHAT FOR / WHERE TO: ESTUDIO PARA APRENDER (I study to learn). POR answers WHY / HOW MUCH / THROUGH: POR LA MAÑANA (in the morning), POR FAVOR (please!).

examples.en: I bought it for ten euros.

mistakes: Saying POR TI for a gift — gifts are PARA ti.
Saying PARA LA LLUVIA for cause — because of = POR.

lessons.title: El correo formal: asunto, saludo, despedida
lessons.learn: A Spanish business email is framed: ASUNTO with the matter, ESTIMADO/A + surname, body, and ATENTAMENTE or UN SALUDO. «Estimados señores» opens to a company.

grammar.title: Email frame
grammar.pattern: Asunto: … · Estimada Sra. Ruiz: · Adjunto … · Quedo a la espera de su respuesta. · Atentamente
grammar.explain: Asunto: Reunión del 12 de mayo. Estimada Sra. Ruiz: Adjunto los documentos. Quedo a la espera de su respuesta antes del viernes. Atentamente. The colon after the greeting is the peninsular convention.

mistakes.why: A first business contact takes the formal greeting and a colon.
The formal register keeps usted and no exclamation marks.

dialogue.en: Is the email all right?

dialogue.t: Falta el asunto, y el saludo es muy informal.
dialogue.r: FAHL-tah el ah-SOON-toh, ee el sah-LOO-doh es mooy een-for-MAL.
dialogue.en: The subject is missing, and the greeting is too informal.
'Dear Mr García'?

dialogue.t: Mejor «Estimado Sr. García:», y al final «Atentamente».
dialogue.r: meh-HOR es-tee-MAH-doh SEH-nyor gar-SEE-ah:, ee al fee-NAL ah-ten-tah-MEN-teh.
dialogue.en: Better 'Dear Mr García:' and at the end 'Yours faithfully'.

grammar.title: Attribution
grammar.pattern: según + source · fuentes cercanas a … · está sin confirmar
grammar.explain: Según el ministerio, los precios suben. Fuentes cercanas a la empresa lo niegan. «según» keeps the claim with the source and is the honest part of the sentence.

culture.text: Spanish argument lives in the tertulia — the regular gathering where talk is the point, and disagreement is expected to be lively and personal without being rude. In writing the tone drops: an opinion piece can concede in the first paragraph («es cierto que…») and then rebut at length, because the concession is read as seriousness rather than weakness. B2 teaches that register: concede, qualify, rebut, propose.

reading.text: «Es cierto que la medida es popular», escribe la columnista, «pero también es cierta una cosa: nadie ha medido su coste.» En la tertulia de la radio la discusión sigue el mismo patrón: primero se concede, después se matiza y solo al final se propone. Alguien dice: «A mí me da la impresión de que el problema no es la norma, sino cómo se aplica.» Y todos están de acuerdo.
reading.gloss: 'It is true that the measure is popular,' writes the columnist, 'but one thing is also true: nobody has measured its cost.' On the radio tertulia the discussion follows the same pattern: first concede, then qualify, and only at the end propose. Someone says: 'It seems to me that the problem is not the rule but how it is applied.' And everyone agrees.

listening.script:
Moderador: ¿Le parece bien la medida?
Ana: En principio sí, aunque tengo dudas.
Moderador: ¿Cuáles?
Ana: No está claro cómo se va a financiar. Por eso propongo medirlo antes.
listening.gloss: Moderator: Do you think the measure is a good idea? Ana: In principle yes, although I have doubts. Moderator: Which ones? Ana: It is not clear how it will be financed. That is why I propose measuring it first.

task.title: Argue one point through four moves
task.instructions: Pick a rule in your workplace or study programme and write four Spanish paragraphs: the point, the concession («es cierto que…»), the objection with a qualifier («aunque», «sin embargo»), and the test or compromise you propose. Then say it aloud in two minutes without notes. Every sentence that starts with a concession should have its verb in the right mood — indicative for a fact, subjunctive for a hypothesis.
